titre: It wasn't television that dismantled the Hollywood studios
accroche: In 1948, the Supreme Court bars the studios from forcing their films on theaters in bulk, opening the way to separating them from the theaters they own.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1948, in most large American cities, a moviegoer who wants to see Paramount's latest film often has only one theater where he can: the one Paramount owns itself. Hollywood's five biggest studios don't just make films. They also hold, at the same time, the theaters that show them.

## A suit against eight studios

The Hollywood film industry between the wars rests on vertical integration: the same companies produce films, distribute them, and own the theaters that show them. Five of them, Paramount, Loew's (MGM), Warner Bros., 20th Century-Fox, and RKO, the “Big Five,” also hold the most profitable theater chains; three others, Universal, Columbia, and United Artists, the “Little Three,” produce and distribute without exhibiting. To keep independent theaters dependent on them, the eight impose block booking: an exhibitor who wants a hit film has to rent a whole package, sight unseen, often for an entire season.

In 1938, the Department of Justice sues the eight studios for violating the Sherman Act, the 1890 antitrust law. The case *United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc.* reaches the Supreme Court, which rules on May 3, 1948 (334 U.S. 131), in an opinion written by Justice William O. Douglas. The Court finds block booking illegal. On vertical integration, it does not condemn it in itself, but only when it is, in the Court's own words, “a calculated scheme to gain control over an appreciable segment of the market.” It notes that, in the 92 American cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants, at least 70% of first-run theaters are affiliated with one or more of the five majors, and that in 38 of these cities there is no independent first-run theater at all. The Court does not itself order the breakup: it reverses part of the trial court's judgment and sends the question of separating production from exhibition back to the district court. Between 1949 and 1952, each studio signs its own consent decree with the Department of Justice, Paramount first, on March 3, 1949, agreeing to sell off its theaters.

## What this changes

The collapse of the old studio system is usually attributed to the arrival of television in American homes in the 1950s. But television did not take hold en masse until after this decision had already begun to dismantle the economic foundation of the system: the legal separation between those who make films and those who own the theaters where they are shown. Television aggravates a decline whose primary cause is legal, not merely cultural. And it is this same fragmentation of theater ownership that, in the following decades, leaves room for independent producers and for the art-house theaters that television competition alone would not have been enough to create.

repere.texte: The Supreme Court itself quantifies the studios' grip on exhibition: “In the 92 cities of the country with populations over 100,000 at least 70 per cent of all the first-run theatres are affiliated with one or more of the five majors” and, in 38 of these cities, there is no independent first-run theater.
repere.source: United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc., 334 U.S. 131 (1948), opinion of Justice William O. Douglas

carte.punch: In 1948, the Supreme Court, not television, broke the Hollywood studio system.
carte.idee: The end of the old Hollywood studio system is attributed to television. But in 1948, the Supreme Court already bars the studios from forcing their films on theaters in packages, and opens the way to separating those who produce films from those who own the theaters.
carte.source_courte: United States v. Paramount Pictures, 334 U.S. 131, 1948

quiz.question: Why does the Supreme Court find, in 1948, that the structure of the big Hollywood studios violates competition law?
choix: Because they refuse to show films by foreign filmmakers in their own theaters
Because they impose block booking and aim to control the market through vertical integration
Because they jointly fund an internal censorship of scripts, the Hays Code
Because they refuse to adapt their theaters to new fire safety standards
quiz.explication: The ruling specifically condemns block booking and a vertical integration organized, in its own terms, as a calculated scheme to control an appreciable segment of the market. Hays Code censorship, safety standards, and foreign films are not the subject of this antitrust case.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the figures cited by the Supreme Court about the 92 American cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants reveal?
choix: Fewer than 10% of first-run theaters are affiliated with them, with most remaining independent
At least 70% of these theaters are affiliated with the five majors, and 38 cities have no independent theater
All of these cities have at least three independent first-run theaters
Independent theaters are broadly in the majority everywhere there, with no notable exception
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court notes that at least 70% of the first-run theaters in these 92 cities are affiliated with one or more of the five majors, and that 38 of these cities have no independent first-run theater.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the Supreme Court order on May 3, 1948, regarding the separation of production from theatrical exhibition?
choix: It orders the complete and immediate separation of the eight studios in question itself
It rejects any idea of separation and instead confirms vertical integration
It reverses part of the judgment and sends the question back to the district court
It refers the entire case to Congress, to legislate anew
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court does not itself order the separation: it reverses part of the trial court's judgment and sends the question of separating production from exhibition back to the district court, which would lead to the consent decrees each studio signed between 1949 and 1952.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which studio is the first to sign its consent decree after the 1948 ruling, and on what date?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Paramount is the first to sign its consent decree, on March 3, 1949; the other studios follow between 1950 and 1952.
